questions.stem: A hydrogen sulfate ion, HSO₄⁻, donates a proton to a water molecule. Which conjugate base forms?
questions.explanation: A conjugate base is what remains after an acid donates one proton. Removing H⁺ from HSO₄⁻ leaves SO₄²⁻. H₂SO₄ is the conjugate acid of HSO₄⁻, formed when it gains a proton.

questions.stem: An ammonia molecule, NH₃, accepts a proton from a water molecule. Which conjugate acid forms?
questions.explanation: A conjugate acid forms when a base accepts one proton. NH₃ + H⁺ gives NH₄⁺. NH₂⁻ is the conjugate base of NH₃, formed when it loses a proton.

questions.stem: CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). Which are the two conjugate acid-base pairs?
options: CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻; H₃O⁺ and H₂O
CH₃COOH and H₂O; CH₃COO⁻ and H₃O⁺
CH₃COOH and H₃O⁺; H₂O and CH₃COO⁻
CH₃COO⁻ and H₂O; CH₃COOH and H₃O⁺
questions.explanation: The two members of a conjugate pair differ by exactly one proton. CH₃COOH loses H⁺ to become CH₃COO⁻, and H₂O gains H⁺ to become H₃O⁺. Pairing the two reactants together is a common error.

questions.stem: In aqueous solution, H⁺(aq) is often written as H₃O⁺(aq). What does H₃O⁺ represent?
options: A hydroxide ion that has gained two extra protons
A water molecule that has lost a single electron
An oxygen atom bonded to three hydrogen ions
A hydronium ion: a proton bonded to a water molecule
questions.explanation: A bare proton cannot exist alone in water; it attaches to a lone pair on a water molecule to form H₃O⁺, the hydronium ion. H⁺(aq) and H₃O⁺(aq) are two ways of writing the same species.

questions.stem: Which species is amphiprotic, able to act as either a Brønsted-Lowry acid or base?
questions.explanation: HCO₃⁻ can donate a proton to become CO₃²⁻ or accept one to become H₂CO₃. CO₃²⁻ has no proton to donate, and NH₄⁺ cannot accept another proton, so each can act only one way.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the hydrogen carbonate ion acting as a Brønsted-Lowry base in water?
questions.explanation: As a base, HCO₃⁻ accepts a proton from water, forming H₂CO₃ and leaving OH⁻. In the equations forming CO₃²⁻, HCO₃⁻ donates a proton, so it is acting as an acid.

questions.stem: Phosphoric acid, H₃PO₄, is a triprotic weak acid. Which equation shows its first ionisation in water?
questions.explanation: A polyprotic acid donates its protons one at a time, each in its own equilibrium. The first step removes one proton to give H₂PO₄⁻. Losing all three protons at once, with a one-way arrow, would describe a strong acid ionising completely.

questions.stem: For a diprotic acid H₂A, why is the second ionisation, HA⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + A²⁻, much smaller than the first?
options: The second ionisation is a reduction, so it needs a source of electrons
Removing a proton from a negative ion is harder than from a neutral molecule
The second proton is always bonded to carbon, so it cannot be donated
The first ionisation uses up all the water, so none is left for the second
questions.explanation: After the first proton leaves, the remaining HA⁻ is negatively charged and attracts the second proton more strongly, so Ka for the second step is much smaller. Both steps are proton transfers, not redox reactions.

questions.stem: Which pair of equations correctly shows a strong acid and a weak acid in water?
options: HCl + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ and HF + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + F⁻
HCl + H₂O → H₂Cl⁺ + OH⁻ and HF + H₂O ⇌ H₂F⁺ + OH⁻
HCl → H₂ + Cl₂ and HF + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + F⁻
HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ and HF + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + F⁻
questions.explanation: A strong acid such as HCl ionises completely, shown by a single arrow. A weak acid such as HF ionises only partly, reaching an equilibrium shown by the double arrow. Acids donate protons to water; they do not accept them.

questions.stem: What is the acidity constant expression, Ka, for hydrofluoric acid, HF(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + F⁻(aq)?
questions.explanation: Products go on top and reactants underneath. Water is the solvent, so its concentration is effectively constant and is incorporated into Ka rather than written in the expression.

questions.stem: Three monoprotic acids at 25 °C have Ka values: HX 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, HY 6.8 × 10⁻⁴ and HZ 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰. Which lists them from strongest to weakest?
questions.explanation: A larger Ka means the acid ionises to a greater extent, so it is stronger. 6.8 × 10⁻⁴ is the largest and 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ the smallest. Comparing the numbers before the powers of ten, ignoring the exponents, gives the wrong order.

questions.stem: Acid HP has Ka = 1 × 10⁻⁴ and acid HQ has Ka = 1 × 10⁻⁸. Which statement about their conjugate bases is correct?
options: Q⁻ is a stronger base than P⁻, because HQ holds its proton more tightly
P⁻ is a stronger base than Q⁻, because HP is the stronger acid
P⁻ and Q⁻ are equally strong, because both acids are monoprotic
Neither is a base, because the conjugates of weak acids cannot accept protons
questions.explanation: The weaker the acid, the more readily its conjugate base takes back a proton. HQ is the weaker acid, with the smaller Ka, so Q⁻ is the stronger conjugate base. Conjugates of weak acids are weak bases, not non-bases.

questions.stem: In a 0.10 mol/L solution of a weak acid HA, about 1% of the HA molecules are ionised. What does this tell you?
options: The solution is dilute, because only 1% of the acid has been dissolved
The acid is strong, because some of its molecules ionise in water
Most of the acid is present as HA molecules, with few H₃O⁺ and A⁻ ions
Most of the acid is present as H₃O⁺ and A⁻ ions, with few HA molecules
questions.explanation: A weak acid ionises only slightly, so the equilibrium lies to the left and nearly all the acid remains as HA. Strength describes the extent of ionisation; concentration describes how much acid is dissolved per litre.

questions.stem: A weak acid solution is diluted with water. What happens to the percentage of acid molecules that are ionised?
options: It stays the same, because Ka does not change when the solution is diluted
It falls to zero, because a dilute acid can no longer donate any protons
It increases, because dilution shifts the ionisation equilibrium to the right
It decreases, because there are fewer acid molecules per litre to ionise
questions.explanation: Diluting lowers every concentration, and the side with more dissolved particles, H₃O⁺ + A⁻, is favoured to partly offset this. Ka stays constant, but the fraction ionised rises. The [H₃O⁺] still falls overall, so the pH rises.

questions.stem: What is the ionic product of water, Kw, at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Water self-ionises slightly, H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻, and Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C in any aqueous solution. 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol/L is the concentration of each ion in pure water.

questions.stem: In pure water at 25 °C, what is the concentration of hydrogen ions?
options: Zero, as pure water has no ions
questions.explanation: Each water molecule that ionises gives one H⁺ and one OH⁻, so [H⁺] = [OH⁻] and [H⁺]² = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, giving 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol/L. This makes the pH 7.00.

questions.stem: A solution at 25 °C has [OH⁻] = 0.020 mol/L. What is its [H⁺]?
questions.explanation: [H⁺] = Kw/[OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴/0.020 = 5.0 × 10⁻¹³ mol/L. Multiplying by Kw instead of dividing gives 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ mol/L.

questions.stem: Kw rises with temperature, and at 50 °C pure water has a pH of about 6.6. Which statement about this water is correct?
options: It is acidic, because heating removes OH⁻ ions
It is neutral, because [H⁺] still equals [OH⁻]
It is acidic, because its pH is below 7
It is basic, because heating forms extra OH⁻
questions.explanation: Heating shifts the endothermic self-ionisation of water to the right, increasing both [H⁺] and [OH⁻] equally. The water is still neutral; only at 25 °C does neutral correspond to pH 7.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.010 mol/L hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: HCl is a strong monoprotic acid, so [H⁺] = 0.010 mol/L and pH = −log(0.010) = 2.00. A pH of 12.00 would be a basic solution.

questions.stem: A solution of nitric acid, a strong monoprotic acid, has a concentration of 0.040 mol/L. What is its pH?
questions.explanation: Nitric acid ionises completely, so [H⁺] = 0.040 mol/L and pH = −log(0.040) = 1.40. Reading the 4 in the concentration as the pH gives 4.00, and 12.60 would be the pH of a 0.040 mol/L strong base.

questions.stem: A sample of rainwater is measured with a pH meter and has a pH of 3.40. What is its [H⁺]?
questions.explanation: [H⁺] = 10^(−pH) = 10^(−3.40) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L. The concentration lies between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻³ mol/L, as expected for a pH between 3 and 4.

questions.stem: Solution P has pH 3 and solution Q has pH 5. How do their hydrogen ion concentrations compare?
options: [H⁺] in Q is 100 times that in P
[H⁺] in P is 0.6 times that in Q
[H⁺] in P is 100 times that in Q
[H⁺] in P is 2 times that in Q
questions.explanation: The pH scale is logarithmic: each unit is a factor of 10 in [H⁺]. P is 2 pH units lower, so its [H⁺] is 10² = 100 times greater.

questions.stem: 10.0 mL of hydrochloric acid with pH 2.00 is diluted with water to 100.0 mL. What is the new pH?
questions.explanation: Diluting tenfold lowers [H⁺] from 1.0 × 10⁻² to 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/L, so the pH rises by one unit to 3.00. Diluting an acid can never lower its pH.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.010 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: [OH⁻] = 0.010 mol/L, so [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴/0.010 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² mol/L and pH = 12.00. Taking −log of [OH⁻] gives 2.00, which is the pOH, not the pH.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.050 mol/L potassium hydroxide solution at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴/0.050 = 2.0 × 10⁻¹³ mol/L, so pH = −log(2.0 × 10⁻¹³) = 12.70. Stopping at −log[OH⁻] gives 1.30.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.0050 mol/L barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)₂, solution at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Each Ba(OH)₂ releases two OH⁻ ions, so [OH⁻] = 0.010 mol/L. [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴/0.010 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² mol/L, giving pH 12.00. Forgetting the factor of two gives 11.70.

questions.stem: A solution at 25 °C has [H⁺] = [OH⁻]. How is it described?
questions.explanation: A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻]. At 25 °C both are 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol/L and the pH is 7.00. An acidic solution has [H⁺] greater than [OH⁻].

questions.stem: In calculating the pH of a weak acid HA from its Ka, two approximations are usually made. What are they?
options: [A⁻] = 0, and the equilibrium [H⁺] equals the initial concentration
[H⁺] = [A⁻], and the equilibrium [HA] equals the initial concentration
[H⁺] = [HA], and the equilibrium [A⁻] equals the initial concentration
[H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol/L, and the acid is fully ionised in water
questions.explanation: Each HA that ionises gives one H⁺ and one A⁻, and the H⁺ from water is negligible, so [H⁺] = [A⁻]. Because so little HA ionises, its equilibrium concentration is taken as its initial value. Then Ka = [H⁺]²/c.

questions.stem: A weak monoprotic acid HA has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is the pH of a 0.10 mol/L solution?
questions.explanation: [H⁺]² = Ka × c = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶, so [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/L and pH = 3.00. Treating the acid as strong gives pH 1.00, and forgetting the square root gives 6.00.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid has Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. What is the pH of 0.10 mol/L ethanoic acid?
questions.explanation: [H⁺] = √(Ka × c) = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol/L, so pH = 2.87. Without the square root, −log(1.8 × 10⁻⁶) gives 5.74; treating the acid as strong gives 1.00.

questions.stem: A weak monoprotic acid with Ka = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ is made up at 0.040 mol/L. What is its pH?
questions.explanation: [H⁺]² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.040 = 1.6 × 10⁻⁷, so [H⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L and pH = 3.40. Assuming full ionisation would give pH 1.40, and skipping the square root gives 6.80.

questions.stem: A 0.10 mol/L solution of a weak monoprotic acid has a pH of 3.00. What is Ka for the acid?
questions.explanation: [H⁺] = [A⁻] = 10⁻³ mol/L, and [HA] is about 0.10 mol/L. Ka = (10⁻³)²/0.10 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. Forgetting to divide by [HA] gives 1.0 × 10⁻⁶.

questions.stem: Equal volumes of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid have the same pH. Which needs more sodium hydroxide to neutralise it completely?
options: Hydrochloric acid, because it is the stronger of the two acids
Both need the same, because they have the same hydrogen ion concentration
Neither can be neutralised, because both are acids of the same pH
Ethanoic acid, because its total concentration of acid is much greater
questions.explanation: For a weak acid to reach the same [H⁺] as a strong acid, its concentration must be far higher, because only a small fraction ionises. As OH⁻ removes H⁺, more ethanoic acid ionises, so all of it is eventually neutralised and much more base is needed.

questions.stem: 0.10 mol/L hydrochloric acid has pH 1.00, but 0.10 mol/L ethanoic acid has pH 2.87. What causes the difference?
options: Hydrochloric acid releases OH⁻ ions as well as H⁺ ions in water
Ethanoic acid ionises only partly, so its [H⁺] is much lower
Ethanoic acid is diprotic, so its protons are released more slowly
Hydrochloric acid is more concentrated than the ethanoic acid
questions.explanation: At the same concentration, a strong acid is fully ionised but a weak acid is only slightly ionised, so it produces far fewer H⁺ ions and has a higher pH. Ethanoic acid is monoprotic.
